title: SELECT Statement
subtitle: Choose student, teacher and marks information from one simple school table.
concept: A SELECT statement shows information stored in a table. Write the column names after SELECT, then write the table name after FROM. In this lesson, the school table has eight students and five easy columns: id, student, teacher, marks and class.

questions.text: Show the name of every student.
questions.solution: SELECT student FROM school;
questions.hint: The student names are in the student column. Select that column from school.
questions.explanation: SELECT student returns the name recorded in each row of the school table.
questions.example: SELECT student FROM school

questions.text: Show the teacher's name for every student.
questions.solution: SELECT teacher FROM school;
questions.hint: Choose the teacher column from the school table.
questions.explanation: The teacher column stores the name of the teacher assigned to each student.
questions.example: SELECT teacher FROM school

questions.text: Show the marks scored by every student.
questions.solution: SELECT marks FROM school;
questions.hint: The marks column contains each student’s score.
questions.explanation: SELECT marks returns the score from every row.
questions.example: SELECT marks FROM school

questions.text: Show each student name with their marks.
questions.solution: SELECT student, marks FROM school;
questions.hint: Select student and marks, separated by a comma.
questions.explanation: You can select more than one column. Write the two column names after SELECT and separate them with a comma.
questions.example: SELECT student, marks FROM school

questions.text: Show all the information stored for every student.
questions.solution: SELECT * FROM school;
questions.hint: Use the * symbol to select every column from school.
questions.explanation: The asterisk (*) means all columns. This returns id, student, teacher, marks and class.
questions.example: SELECT * FROM school

questions.text: Show every student with their class number.
questions.solution: SELECT student, class FROM school;
questions.hint: Choose student and class from school.
questions.explanation: The class column tells which class each student belongs to.
questions.example: SELECT student, class FROM school

questions.text: Show each teacher together with the marks of their students.
questions.solution: SELECT teacher, marks FROM school;
questions.hint: Select teacher and marks from the same table.
questions.explanation: The result shows the teacher name next to the score for each student.
questions.example: SELECT teacher, marks FROM school

questions.text: Show each student with their teacher.
questions.solution: SELECT student, teacher FROM school;
questions.hint: Choose the student and teacher columns.
questions.explanation: This query displays the student name and the assigned teacher side by side.
questions.example: SELECT student, teacher FROM school

questions.text: Show the student name, class and marks.
questions.solution: SELECT student, class, marks FROM school;
questions.hint: Select student, class and marks in that order.
questions.explanation: A SELECT statement can return three columns. Separate each column name with a comma.
questions.example: SELECT student, class, marks FROM school

questions.text: Show the ID and name of every student.
questions.solution: SELECT id, student FROM school;
questions.hint: Select the id and student columns.
questions.explanation: The id is the student record number. The student column stores the name.
questions.example: SELECT id, student FROM school

title: WHERE Clause
subtitle: Find students by their marks, teacher or class.
concept: WHERE filters rows. It keeps only the students whose information matches your condition. Use > to find values above a number, < for values below it, and = to find an exact match.

questions.text: Find the student with a row id of 6.
questions.solution: SELECT id, student FROM school WHERE id = 6;
questions.hint: Use WHERE id = 6 to find the student in row 6.
questions.explanation: The condition id = 6 selects only the row whose id is 6. The result shows both the id (6) and the student name (Ayaan).
questions.example: SELECT id, student FROM school WHERE id = 6

questions.text: Find students who scored less than 70 marks.
questions.solution: SELECT student, marks FROM school WHERE marks < 70;
questions.hint: Use WHERE marks < 70. The < sign means less than.
questions.explanation: Only students with a score below 70 are returned.
questions.example: SELECT student, marks FROM school WHERE marks < 70

questions.text: Find the student who scored exactly 95 marks.
questions.solution: SELECT student, marks FROM school WHERE marks = 95;
questions.hint: Use the equals sign with marks = 95.
questions.explanation: The equals sign finds the row whose marks value is exactly 95.
questions.example: SELECT student, marks FROM school WHERE marks = 95

questions.text: Find all students who are in class 5.
questions.solution: SELECT student, class FROM school WHERE class = 5;
questions.hint: Filter the class column using WHERE class = 5.
questions.explanation: This returns the students whose class value is 5.
questions.example: SELECT student, class FROM school WHERE class = 5

questions.text: Find all students whose teacher is Neha.
questions.solution: SELECT student, teacher FROM school WHERE teacher = 'Neha';
questions.hint: Text values need single quotes: teacher = 'Neha'.
questions.explanation: The condition matches rows where the teacher name is Neha.
questions.example: SELECT student, teacher FROM school WHERE teacher = 'Neha'

questions.text: Find students who scored 90 marks or more.
questions.solution: SELECT student, marks FROM school WHERE marks >= 90;
questions.hint: Use >= to include 90 and any higher score.
questions.explanation: Greater than or equal to includes the boundary value 90.
questions.example: SELECT student, marks FROM school WHERE marks >= 90

questions.text: Find students whose marks are from 70 to 90.
questions.solution: SELECT student, marks FROM school WHERE marks BETWEEN 70 AND 90;
questions.hint: Use BETWEEN 70 AND 90 on the marks column.
questions.explanation: BETWEEN includes both 70 and 90.
questions.example: SELECT student, marks FROM school WHERE marks BETWEEN 70 AND 90

questions.text: Find students taught by Ravi.
questions.solution: SELECT student, teacher FROM school WHERE teacher = 'Ravi';
questions.hint: Compare teacher with the text value Ravi in single quotes.
questions.explanation: This returns students whose teacher is Ravi.
questions.example: SELECT student, teacher FROM school WHERE teacher = 'Ravi'

questions.text: Find students who are in class 6.
questions.solution: SELECT student, class FROM school WHERE class = 6;
questions.hint: Use WHERE class = 6.
questions.explanation: The filter keeps only students in class 6.
questions.example: SELECT student, class FROM school WHERE class = 6

questions.text: Find students who scored exactly 68 marks.
questions.solution: SELECT student, marks FROM school WHERE marks = 68;
questions.hint: Use an exact match: marks = 68.
questions.explanation: The query returns the student row with 68 marks.
questions.example: SELECT student, marks FROM school WHERE marks = 68

title: ORDER BY
subtitle: Put student names and marks in a useful order.
concept: ORDER BY sorts rows using the column you choose. ASC means ascending (low to high or A to Z). DESC means descending (high to low or Z to A).

questions.text: Show students from the highest marks to the lowest.
questions.solution: SELECT student, marks FROM school ORDER BY marks DESC;
questions.hint: Sort the marks column using DESC.
questions.explanation: DESC puts the highest score first.
questions.example: SELECT student, marks FROM school ORDER BY marks DESC

questions.text: Show students from the lowest marks to the highest.
questions.solution: SELECT student, marks FROM school ORDER BY marks ASC;
questions.hint: Sort marks using ASC.
questions.explanation: ASC puts the smallest score first.
questions.example: SELECT student, marks FROM school ORDER BY marks ASC

questions.text: Show student names from A to Z.
questions.solution: SELECT student FROM school ORDER BY student ASC;
questions.hint: Sort the student column in ascending order.
questions.explanation: ASC sorts text from A to Z.
questions.example: SELECT student FROM school ORDER BY student ASC

questions.text: Show students from class 5 first, then class 6.
questions.solution: SELECT student, class FROM school ORDER BY class ASC;
questions.hint: Sort by class using ASC.
questions.explanation: Ascending order places class 5 before class 6.
questions.example: SELECT student, class FROM school ORDER BY class ASC

questions.text: Show the three students with the highest marks, highest first.
questions.solution: SELECT student, marks FROM school ORDER BY marks DESC LIMIT 3;
questions.hint: Sort marks from highest to lowest, then use LIMIT 3.
questions.explanation: ORDER BY sorts the marks and LIMIT keeps the first three rows.
questions.example: SELECT student, marks FROM school ORDER BY marks DESC LIMIT 3

questions.text: Show teacher names from A to Z.
questions.solution: SELECT teacher FROM school ORDER BY teacher ASC;
questions.hint: Sort the teacher column using ASC.
questions.explanation: Teacher names appear in alphabetical order.
questions.example: SELECT teacher FROM school ORDER BY teacher ASC

questions.text: Show student names from Z to A.
questions.solution: SELECT student FROM school ORDER BY student DESC;
questions.hint: Use DESC to reverse the alphabetical order.
questions.explanation: DESC sorts names from Z to A.
questions.example: SELECT student FROM school ORDER BY student DESC

questions.text: Show the two students with the lowest marks.
questions.solution: SELECT student, marks FROM school ORDER BY marks ASC LIMIT 2;
questions.hint: Sort marks from low to high and use LIMIT 2.
questions.explanation: This returns the two smallest marks.
questions.example: SELECT student, marks FROM school ORDER BY marks ASC LIMIT 2

questions.text: Show students by class, then by name.
questions.solution: SELECT student, class FROM school ORDER BY class ASC, student ASC;
questions.hint: Use two sort columns: class first, then student.
questions.explanation: SQL sorts by class first and uses student name to order rows within each class.
questions.example: SELECT student, class FROM school ORDER BY class ASC, student ASC

questions.text: Show the top four marks, highest first.
questions.solution: SELECT marks FROM school ORDER BY marks DESC LIMIT 4;
questions.hint: Sort marks in descending order and limit to four rows.
questions.explanation: The result contains the four highest marks.
questions.example: SELECT marks FROM school ORDER BY marks DESC LIMIT 4

title: DISTINCT & LIMIT
subtitle: See teacher names once and control how many school records are shown.
concept: DISTINCT removes repeated values from the result. LIMIT sets the maximum number of rows to show. The school table has repeated teacher names, so it is useful for practising DISTINCT.

questions.text: Show each teacher name only once.
questions.solution: SELECT DISTINCT teacher FROM school;
questions.hint: Put DISTINCT immediately after SELECT.
questions.explanation: DISTINCT removes repeated teacher names, so each teacher appears once.
questions.example: SELECT DISTINCT teacher FROM school

questions.text: Show each class number only once.
questions.solution: SELECT DISTINCT class FROM school;
questions.hint: Use DISTINCT with the class column.
questions.explanation: Some students are in the same class. DISTINCT shows each class value one time.
questions.example: SELECT DISTINCT class FROM school

questions.text: Show the first five student names in ID order.
questions.solution: SELECT student FROM school ORDER BY id LIMIT 5;
questions.hint: Sort by id, then use LIMIT 5.
questions.explanation: ORDER BY id gives a clear row order. LIMIT 5 returns only the first five names.
questions.example: SELECT student FROM school ORDER BY id LIMIT 5

questions.text: Show the first three student names from A to Z.
questions.solution: SELECT student FROM school ORDER BY student ASC LIMIT 3;
questions.hint: Sort student in ascending order, then limit to three rows.
questions.explanation: ASC sorts names alphabetically. LIMIT 3 keeps only the first three names.
questions.example: SELECT student FROM school ORDER BY student ASC LIMIT 3

questions.text: Show the three highest marks.
questions.solution: SELECT marks FROM school ORDER BY marks DESC LIMIT 3;
questions.hint: Sort marks from highest to lowest and show three rows.
questions.explanation: DESC places the largest marks first. LIMIT 3 returns the top three scores.
questions.example: SELECT marks FROM school ORDER BY marks DESC LIMIT 3

questions.text: Show each marks value only once.
questions.solution: SELECT DISTINCT marks FROM school;
questions.hint: Use DISTINCT with marks.
questions.explanation: DISTINCT removes repeated score values.
questions.example: SELECT DISTINCT marks FROM school

questions.text: Show the first four student names by ID.
questions.solution: SELECT student FROM school ORDER BY id LIMIT 4;
questions.hint: Order by id and limit the result to four rows.
questions.explanation: LIMIT 4 keeps the first four records in ID order.
questions.example: SELECT student FROM school ORDER BY id LIMIT 4

questions.text: Show the top five students and their marks, highest marks first.
questions.solution: SELECT student, marks FROM school ORDER BY marks DESC LIMIT 5;
questions.hint: Select student and marks, sort by marks DESC, and add LIMIT 5.
questions.explanation: This returns the five highest scores with each student name.
questions.example: SELECT student, marks FROM school ORDER BY marks DESC LIMIT 5

questions.text: Show each teacher name once in A-to-Z order.
questions.solution: SELECT DISTINCT teacher FROM school ORDER BY teacher ASC;
questions.hint: Use DISTINCT teacher and then ORDER BY teacher ASC.
questions.explanation: DISTINCT removes duplicates and ORDER BY sorts the remaining names.
questions.example: SELECT DISTINCT teacher FROM school ORDER BY teacher ASC

questions.text: Show the two lowest marks.
questions.solution: SELECT marks FROM school ORDER BY marks ASC LIMIT 2;
questions.hint: Sort marks from low to high and limit to two rows.
questions.explanation: ASC places the smallest score first. LIMIT 2 returns two scores.
questions.example: SELECT marks FROM school ORDER BY marks ASC LIMIT 2

title: Filtering & Conditions
subtitle: Use text comparisons, lists and pattern matching in WHERE.
concept: WHERE can compare text exactly with =, != or <>. LIKE and NOT LIKE match text patterns; % stands for zero or more characters and _ stands for exactly one character. IN and NOT IN check whether a text value is inside or outside a list. In this SQLite practice database, LIKE is case-insensitive for ordinary ASCII text by default.

questions.text: Find students whose teacher is exactly Neha using =.
questions.solution: SELECT student, teacher FROM school WHERE teacher = 'Neha';
questions.hint: Use = for an exact text match and put the text in single quotes: teacher = 'Neha'.
questions.explanation: = compares the text exactly. With the default SQLite collation used here, this match is case-sensitive.
questions.example: SELECT student, teacher FROM school WHERE teacher = 'Neha'

questions.text: Find students whose teacher is not Neha using !=.
questions.solution: SELECT student, teacher FROM school WHERE teacher != 'Neha';
questions.hint: Use != to find text values that are not equal to 'Neha'.
questions.explanation: != is the not-equal operator. It returns rows whose teacher value is different from Neha.
questions.example: SELECT student, teacher FROM school WHERE teacher != 'Neha'

questions.text: Find students whose name is not Aarav using <>.
questions.solution: SELECT student FROM school WHERE student <> 'Aarav';
questions.hint: <> also means not equal to. Compare student with the quoted text 'Aarav'.
questions.explanation: <> and != are two spellings of the same not-equal comparison in SQL.
questions.example: SELECT student FROM school WHERE student <> 'Aarav'

questions.text: Find students whose teacher matches NEHA using LIKE.
questions.solution: SELECT student, teacher FROM school WHERE teacher LIKE 'NEHA';
questions.hint: Use LIKE 'NEHA'. In this SQLite lesson, LIKE matches ordinary ASCII text without case sensitivity by default.
questions.explanation: LIKE can compare text without case sensitivity for ordinary ASCII letters in this SQLite practice database. Without wildcards, it checks the whole value.
questions.example: SELECT student, teacher FROM school WHERE teacher LIKE 'NEHA'

questions.text: Find students whose teacher does not match NEHA using NOT LIKE.
questions.solution: SELECT student, teacher FROM school WHERE teacher NOT LIKE 'NEHA';
questions.hint: Use NOT LIKE 'NEHA' to exclude that text match.
questions.explanation: NOT LIKE returns rows that do not match the pattern. In this database the comparison is case-insensitive for ordinary ASCII letters.
questions.example: SELECT student, teacher FROM school WHERE teacher NOT LIKE 'NEHA'

questions.text: Find students whose names start with A using the % wildcard.
questions.solution: SELECT student FROM school WHERE student LIKE 'A%';
questions.hint: A% means the name starts with A and can have any number of characters after it.
questions.explanation: % matches a sequence of zero or more characters. It is used with LIKE or NOT LIKE.
questions.example: SELECT student FROM school WHERE student LIKE 'A%'

questions.text: Find students whose names start with A and have exactly five characters using _.
questions.solution: SELECT student FROM school WHERE student LIKE 'A____';
questions.hint: After A, write four underscores. Each underscore matches exactly one character.
questions.explanation: _ matches exactly one character. A____ means A followed by exactly four more characters.
questions.example: SELECT student FROM school WHERE student LIKE 'A____'

questions.text: Find students taught by either Neha or Ravi using IN.
questions.solution: SELECT student, teacher FROM school WHERE teacher IN ('Neha', 'Ravi');
questions.hint: Put both teacher names in the IN list and quote each name.
questions.explanation: IN checks whether the teacher value matches one of the values in the list. It is a shorter way to express these alternatives with OR.
questions.example: SELECT student, teacher FROM school WHERE teacher IN ('Neha', 'Ravi')

questions.text: Find students whose teacher is neither Neha nor Ravi using NOT IN.
questions.solution: SELECT student, teacher FROM school WHERE teacher NOT IN ('Neha', 'Ravi');
questions.hint: Use NOT IN with a list containing 'Neha' and 'Ravi'.
questions.explanation: NOT IN keeps rows whose teacher value does not appear in the supplied list.
questions.example: SELECT student, teacher FROM school WHERE teacher NOT IN ('Neha', 'Ravi')

questions.text: Find students whose teacher name starts with N and who are in class 5.
questions.solution: SELECT student, teacher, class FROM school WHERE teacher LIKE 'N%' AND class = 5;
questions.hint: Use LIKE 'N%' for the teacher name and join it with class = 5 using AND.
questions.explanation: This combines a text pattern with another WHERE condition. AND requires both conditions to be true.
questions.example: SELECT student, teacher, class FROM school WHERE teacher LIKE 'N%' AND class = 5

questions.text: Find students whose marks are above 80 AND whose class is 5.
questions.solution: SELECT student, marks, class FROM school WHERE marks > 80 AND class = 5;
questions.hint: Use AND to require both conditions.
questions.explanation: Use the SQL operator named in the task to filter rows from the school table.
questions.example: SELECT student, marks, class FROM school WHERE marks > 80 AND class = 5

questions.text: Find students whose teacher is Neha OR whose teacher is Ravi.
questions.solution: SELECT student, teacher FROM school WHERE teacher = 'Neha' OR teacher = 'Ravi';
questions.hint: Use OR when either condition can match.
questions.explanation: Use the SQL operator named in the task to filter rows from the school table.
questions.example: SELECT student, teacher FROM school WHERE teacher = 'Neha' OR teacher = 'Ravi'

questions.text: Find students who are NOT in class 5.
questions.solution: SELECT student, class FROM school WHERE NOT class = 5;
questions.hint: NOT reverses the condition.
questions.explanation: Use the SQL operator named in the task to filter rows from the school table.
questions.example: SELECT student, class FROM school WHERE NOT class = 5

questions.text: Find students with marks above 80 AND teacher Neha.
questions.solution: SELECT student, marks, teacher FROM school WHERE marks > 80 AND teacher = 'Neha';
questions.hint: Both conditions must be true.
questions.explanation: Use the SQL operator named in the task to filter rows from the school table.
questions.example: SELECT student, marks, teacher FROM school WHERE marks > 80 AND teacher = 'Neha'

questions.text: Find students in class 5 OR students with marks below 70.
questions.solution: SELECT student, class, marks FROM school WHERE class = 5 OR marks < 70;
questions.hint: Either condition can match.
questions.explanation: Use the SQL operator named in the task to filter rows from the school table.
questions.example: SELECT student, class, marks FROM school WHERE class = 5 OR marks < 70

questions.text: Find students whose teacher is NOT Imran.
questions.solution: SELECT student, teacher FROM school WHERE NOT teacher = 'Imran';
questions.hint: NOT reverses the teacher comparison.
questions.explanation: Use the SQL operator named in the task to filter rows from the school table.
questions.example: SELECT student, teacher FROM school WHERE NOT teacher = 'Imran'

questions.text: Find students in class 6 AND with marks of at least 80.
questions.solution: SELECT student, class, marks FROM school WHERE class = 6 AND marks >= 80;
questions.hint: Use AND with both conditions.
questions.explanation: Use the SQL operator named in the task to filter rows from the school table.
questions.example: SELECT student, class, marks FROM school WHERE class = 6 AND marks >= 80

questions.text: Find students taught by Neha OR students in class 6.
questions.solution: SELECT student, teacher, class FROM school WHERE teacher = 'Neha' OR class = 6;
questions.hint: OR accepts either condition.
questions.explanation: Use the SQL operator named in the task to filter rows from the school table.

questions.text: Find students who are NOT in class 6 AND have marks above 60.

questions.explanation: Use the SQL operator named in the task to filter rows from the school table.

questions.text: Find students whose marks are BETWEEN 70 AND 90.
questions.solution: SELECT student, marks FROM school WHERE marks BETWEEN 70 AND 90;
questions.hint: BETWEEN includes both boundary values.
questions.explanation: Use the SQL operator named in the task to filter rows from the school table.
questions.example: SELECT student, marks FROM school WHERE marks BETWEEN 70 AND 90

questions.text: Find students whose marks are NOT BETWEEN 70 AND 90.
questions.solution: SELECT student, marks FROM school WHERE marks NOT BETWEEN 70 AND 90;
questions.hint: NOT BETWEEN excludes the range.
questions.explanation: Use the SQL operator named in the task to filter rows from the school table.
questions.example: SELECT student, marks FROM school WHERE marks NOT BETWEEN 70 AND 90

questions.text: Find students in class 5 or class 6 using IN.
questions.solution: SELECT student, class FROM school WHERE class IN (5, 6);
questions.hint: IN checks a list of allowed values.
questions.explanation: Use the SQL operator named in the task to filter rows from the school table.

questions.text: Find students whose teacher is not Neha or Ravi using NOT IN.
questions.solution: SELECT student, teacher FROM school WHERE teacher NOT IN ('Neha', 'Ravi');
questions.hint: NOT IN excludes every listed value.
questions.explanation: Use the SQL operator named in the task to filter rows from the school table.

questions.text: Find students with marks BETWEEN 80 AND 95.
questions.solution: SELECT student, marks FROM school WHERE marks BETWEEN 80 AND 95;
questions.hint: Use the lower and upper values with BETWEEN.
questions.explanation: Use the SQL operator named in the task to filter rows from the school table.
questions.example: SELECT student, marks FROM school WHERE marks BETWEEN 80 AND 95

questions.text: Find students whose class is IN (5).
questions.solution: SELECT student, class FROM school WHERE class IN (5);
questions.hint: IN can also check a one-item list.
questions.explanation: Use the SQL operator named in the task to filter rows from the school table.
questions.example: SELECT student, class FROM school WHERE class IN (5)

questions.text: Find students whose marks are NOT BETWEEN 60 AND 80.
questions.solution: SELECT student, marks FROM school WHERE marks NOT BETWEEN 60 AND 80;
questions.hint: Use NOT BETWEEN to exclude the range.
questions.explanation: Use the SQL operator named in the task to filter rows from the school table.
questions.example: SELECT student, marks FROM school WHERE marks NOT BETWEEN 60 AND 80

questions.text: Find students taught by Neha or Imran using IN.
questions.solution: SELECT student, teacher FROM school WHERE teacher IN ('Neha', 'Imran');
questions.hint: Put text values in quotes inside IN.
questions.explanation: Use the SQL operator named in the task to filter rows from the school table.
questions.example: SELECT student, teacher FROM school WHERE teacher IN ('Neha', 'Imran')

questions.text: Find students whose teacher is exactly Ravi using =.
questions.solution: SELECT student, teacher FROM school WHERE teacher = 'Ravi';
questions.hint: Use = for an exact text match.
questions.explanation: Use the SQL operator named in the task to filter rows from the school table.
questions.example: SELECT student, teacher FROM school WHERE teacher = 'Ravi'

questions.text: Find students whose teacher is not Ravi using !=.
questions.solution: SELECT student, teacher FROM school WHERE teacher != 'Ravi';

questions.explanation: Use the SQL operator named in the task to filter rows from the school table.
questions.example: SELECT student, teacher FROM school WHERE teacher != 'Ravi'

questions.text: Find students whose name is not Meera using <>.
questions.solution: SELECT student FROM school WHERE student <> 'Meera';
questions.hint: <> is another not-equal operator.
questions.explanation: Use the SQL operator named in the task to filter rows from the school table.

questions.text: Find the student named Ayaan using =.
questions.solution: SELECT id, student FROM school WHERE student = 'Ayaan';
questions.hint: Match the complete student name.
questions.explanation: Use the SQL operator named in the task to filter rows from the school table.

questions.hint: Compare the teacher column with an exact value.

title: Joins
subtitle: Combine related information from two tables using a shared key.
concept: JOIN connects related rows. An INNER JOIN returns rows where the join condition matches in both tables. Use the matching id columns to connect records.

questions.text: Join students with enrollments using student id.
questions.solution: SELECT students.id, students.name, enrollments.id AS enrollment_id, enrollments.course_id FROM students JOIN enrollments ON students.id = enrollments.student_id;
questions.hint: Match students.id with enrollments.student_id.
questions.explanation: JOIN combines related rows from two tables. The ON expression matches the key in one table with its related key in the other; only matching pairs are returned by this INNER JOIN. AS assigns a temporary, readable label to a result column. It changes the output heading, not the stored column name.

questions.text: Show student names with their course ids.
questions.solution: SELECT students.name, enrollments.course_id FROM students JOIN enrollments ON students.id = enrollments.student_id;
questions.hint: Join students to enrollments through the student id.
questions.explanation: JOIN combines related rows from two tables. The ON expression matches the key in one table with its related key in the other; only matching pairs are returned by this INNER JOIN.

questions.text: Join courses and enrollments using course id.
questions.solution: SELECT courses.id, courses.title, enrollments.id AS enrollment_id, enrollments.student_id FROM courses JOIN enrollments ON courses.id = enrollments.course_id;
questions.hint: Match courses.id with enrollments.course_id.
questions.explanation: JOIN combines related rows from two tables. The ON expression matches the key in one table with its related key in the other; only matching pairs are returned by this INNER JOIN. AS assigns a temporary, readable label to a result column. It changes the output heading, not the stored column name.

questions.text: Show course titles with enrollment status.
questions.solution: SELECT courses.title, enrollments.status FROM courses JOIN enrollments ON courses.id = enrollments.course_id;
questions.hint: Join courses and enrollments, then select title and status.
questions.explanation: JOIN combines related rows from two tables. The ON expression matches the key in one table with its related key in the other; only matching pairs are returned by this INNER JOIN.

questions.text: Show teacher names with their matching department names.
questions.solution: SELECT teachers.name, departments.department_name FROM teachers JOIN departments ON teachers.department = departments.department_name;
questions.hint: The text in teachers.department matches departments.department_name.
questions.explanation: JOIN combines related rows from two tables. The ON expression matches the key in one table with its related key in the other; only matching pairs are returned by this INNER JOIN.

questions.text: Join students and courses through enrollments.
questions.solution: SELECT students.name, courses.title FROM students JOIN enrollments ON students.id = enrollments.student_id JOIN courses ON courses.id = enrollments.course_id;
questions.hint: Use enrollments as the bridge between students and courses.
questions.explanation: JOIN combines related rows from two tables. The ON expression matches the key in one table with its related key in the other; only matching pairs are returned by this INNER JOIN.

questions.text: Show student name and enrolled_on date.
questions.solution: SELECT students.name, enrollments.enrolled_on FROM students JOIN enrollments ON students.id = enrollments.student_id;
questions.hint: Join by student id, then select name and enrolled_on.
questions.explanation: JOIN combines related rows from two tables. The ON expression matches the key in one table with its related key in the other; only matching pairs are returned by this INNER JOIN.

questions.text: Show course title and student id for each enrollment.
questions.solution: SELECT courses.title, enrollments.student_id FROM courses JOIN enrollments ON courses.id = enrollments.course_id;
questions.hint: Join on course id and select the course title plus student_id.
questions.explanation: JOIN combines related rows from two tables. The ON expression matches the key in one table with its related key in the other; only matching pairs are returned by this INNER JOIN.

questions.text: Join teachers to courses using teacher_id.

title: GROUP BY and HAVING
subtitle: Group similar rows and filter the resulting groups.
concept: GROUP BY creates one group for each distinct value. HAVING filters groups after aggregation; WHERE filters rows before grouping.

FROM students tells SQL which records to summarize; an alias after AS gives the calculated column a readable name. GROUP BY city puts rows with the same value into one group, allowing an aggregate such as COUNT or AVG to calculate one result per group. AS assigns a temporary, readable label to a result column. It changes the output heading, not the stored column name.

title: Database & Table Basics (DDL)
subtitle: Create tables, choose column types and understand primary keys.
concept: CREATE TABLE defines columns. A PRIMARY KEY uniquely identifies each row. Common SQLite types include INTEGER, TEXT and REAL.

questions.text: Create a books table with id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT.
questions.solution: CREATE TABLE books (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT);
questions.hint: Use CREATE TABLE books (...). Separate column definitions with commas and mark id as PRIMARY KEY.
questions.verify: SELECT type, name, tbl_name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type IN ('table', 'index', 'view', 'trigger') AND name NOT LIKE 'sqlite_%'; SELECT cid, name, upper(type) AS type, "notnull", dflt_value, pk FROM pragma_table_info('books');
questions.explanation: CREATE TABLE defines a new table named books. Each definition gives a column name and a data type. INTEGER stores whole numbers, TEXT stores strings, and REAL stores decimal numbers. PRIMARY KEY marks a column as the row's unique identifier.
questions.displayVerify: SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'table' AND name = 'books'; SELECT name, upper(type) AS type, pk FROM pragma_table_info('books');
